query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix, degradation at elevated temperatures is governed by preferential oxidation at grain boundaries that depletes critical elements (e.g., Cr and Ti) and promotes the formation and subsequent spallation of non-protective oxide layers. This intergranular oxidation weakens cohesion between grains, while under reducing environments the suppression of vigorous external oxide formation instead leads to an accumulation of internal defects (e.g., nanovoids) that eventually coalesce, both mechanisms predisposing the alloy to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-produced additive manufactured HEA with a uniform FCC matrix that contains a high density of grain boundaries and residual dislocation structures.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to a controlled high-temperature (800–1000 °C) environment under two different gas atmospheres: one oxidizing (e.g., ~10 mbar oxygen partial pressure) and one reducing (e.g., a hydrogen-rich mixture), while holding all other conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures in the range of 800–1000 °C, exposure durations of 1–5 hours, with gas atmospheres precisely controlled for oxygen partial pressure to simulate oxidizing or reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and intergranular regions where selective oxidation can preferentially occur, leading to local depletion of alloying elements and the potential nucleation of nanovoids.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, grain boundaries rapidly form layered oxide scales that, due to growth stresses, spall off and leave behind embrittled, element-depleted regions that compromise intergranular cohesion. In contrast, in reducing conditions the limited formation of an external oxide permits internal defect accumulation (e.g., nanovoids along grain boundaries) which under thermal and mechanical loading coalesce, again leading to a loss in cohesive strength and catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-manufactured baseline, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will show pronounced oxide scale formation with evidence of spallation and significant intergranular embrittlement (manifested as reduced ductility and earlier crack initiation), while samples under reducing conditions will display fewer surface oxides but an increasing concentration of internal voids and subtle intergranular weakening that eventually precipitate failure.
generation.baseline: The initial as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibiting a uniform FCC matrix with established mechanical properties and no pre-existing significant intergranular oxidation or nanovoid accumulation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for exposures at elevated temperatures between approximately 800 and 1000 °C over durations of 1 to 5 hours under controlled oxidizing (e.g., 10 mbar O2) and reducing (hydrogen-rich) gas atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale growth, the threshold of element depletion needed to compromise grain boundary strength, and the relative contribution of void coalescence under reducing conditions remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identically processed additively manufactured alloy samples. Divide them into three groups: (1) a control group with no elevated-temperature exposure, (2) an oxidizing group exposed to ~10 mbar O2 at 900 °C for 3 hours, and (3) a reducing group exposed to a hydrogen-rich atmosphere under the same thermal conditions. Post-exposure, conduct high-resolution electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to analyze the oxide scale morphology, grain boundary chemistry, and presence of nanovoids. Perform mechanical tensile tests to assess ductility and failure modes.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and spallation characteristics via SEM/TEM
Grain boundary elemental composition (particularly Cr and Ti levels) via EDS
Internal defect (nanovoid) density using high-resolution imaging
Mechanical properties (ductility, fracture strain, and failure mode) via tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If neither the oxidizing nor the reducing exposures show a significant change in grain boundary chemistry (i.e., no measurable depletion of critical elements) or in internal defect concentration relative to the as-manufactured baseline, and if the mechanical failure modes remain unchanged, then the hypothesis—that degradation is governed by intergranular oxidation (or defect accumulation in the absence of oxidation) leading to catastrophic failure—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. Another critical factor leading to the high ductility is the formation of nanovoids in the BCC lamellae during the latter stage of plastic deformation, which turns out to prevent catastrophic failure. In SEM observation (Fig. 5a), nanovoids (~100 nm in diameter) form within the BCC lamellae at a strain of 10%, initiating from the phase boundaries. With increasing strain (15–20%), more nanovoids appear and propagate within the BCC lamellae. Instead of causing rapid rupture of the lamellae, these nanovoids grow under the confinement of the adjacent FCC lamellae (already hardened at this stage), which effectively delays the failure of the alloy. At the final stage of deformation, the coalescence of these nanovoids breaks the constraints of the FCC lamellae, resulting in the fracture of the EHEA (Supplementary Fig. 8a).
